# Start here {#quickstart}

Use this chapter if you are about to submit a paper and need to get the code
behind it ready to share. It covers the minimum steps to turn your project
folder into an archive that someone else can download, open and run.

::: {.tada-key}
Go through the project in four passes, roughly in this order: fix the **paths
and file types**, **archive** it and get a DOI, write the **README**, then
**annotate** the scripts. Finally, ask a colleague to run the whole thing
before a reviewer has to.
:::

## The pre-submission checklist {#quickstart-checklist}

:::: {.tada-checklist-head}
::: {.tada-dog-float}
![](assets/figures/dog-sad.png){.tada-dog-sad alt="A sad cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
![](assets/figures/dog-happy.png){.tada-dog-happy alt="A happy cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
:::

::: {.tada-dog-hint}
Try doing all of these to make the dog happy.
:::
::::

TADA covers your code. The data have their own short list. Tick every box and see what happens.

::: {.tabset}

### Code (TADA) {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Condensed from the TADA guidelines.

**Transferable** — [full chapter](#transferable)

- [ ] Every script is saved with a standard code extension (`.R`, `.py`, `.cpp`, …), not inside a `.docx` or `.pdf`
- [ ] No `setwd()` (R) or `os.chdir()` (Python) appears anywhere in the code
- [ ] No absolute paths (`/Users/you/…`, `C:/Users/you/…`) remain; paths are relative
- [ ] Data, code and materials all live in **one** project directory
- [ ] The project has been opened from a clean start and still runs

**Available** — [full chapter](#available)

- [ ] Code is deposited in an immutable repository that mints a persistent identifier (Zenodo, Figshare, …)
- [ ] The DOI is **cited in the manuscript text and reference list**
- [ ] If the code was developed on GitHub, a release has been created and linked to Zenodo, since GitHub does not produced DOIs

**Documented** — [full chapter](#documented)

- [ ] A `README.md` (or `README.txt`) sits at the top of the project
- [ ] It names the manuscript, the authors, a contact address, and any funders
- [ ] It lists software **and version** (e.g. R v4.3.3) and key packages **and versions** (e.g. ggplot2 v3.5.1)
- [ ] It states the licence
- [ ] It says where the data are, ideally with their own DOI
- [ ] It says what each file is, what order to run things in, what the code needs and what it produces
- [ ] It flags anything slow or resource-hungry
- [ ] A licence is actually attached to the deposit

**Annotated** — [full chapter](#annotated)

- [ ] Code is broken into labelled chunks
- [ ] Each chunk says *what* it does, *why*, and *which* result it produces
- [ ] Signposts point at the manuscript ("produces Figure 3B", "Table 2, column 4")

**Before you submit** — [full chapter](#code-review)

- [ ] Someone else has run the whole project from the archived files, successfully
- [ ] `set.seed()` / `random.seed()` is set before anything stochastic (SORTEE Stage 6, [Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}; not a TADA requirement; see [Code review](#code-review))

### Data {.unlisted .unnumbered}

::: {.tada-wiki}
This is the data counterpart to the code checklist, condensed from the
[SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) and the [Data & code sharing](#data-sharing)
chapter, where every point is explained in full.
:::

**Archived & citable** — [Available](#available)

- [ ] Data deposited in an immutable repository with a DOI, cited in the manuscript text and reference list
- [ ] Nothing lives only in supplementary material

**Present & complete** — [what to share](#sharing-what)

- [ ] Raw data archived — or a sample plus the processed data, or a documented route to obtaining them
- [ ] Processed and filtered data archived, or the code that produces them

**Interoperable format** — [file formats](#sharing-formats)

- [ ] Data in `.csv`, `.tsv`, `.txt` or `.parquet`, not `.xls`, `.sav` or `.pdf`

**Documented** — [metadata](#sharing-metadata)

- [ ] A data README or dictionary describes every file and every variable, **with units**
- [ ] Collection date and location, funders, and any derived-data sources are recorded

**Licensed** — [data licences](#sharing-licences)

- [ ] A data licence is chosen and stated (CC0 or CC BY are the usual choices)

:::

::: {.tada-wiki}
The most useful check on this page is to **download your own archived deposit
into a fresh, empty folder, ideally on a different machine, and run it.** It catches the failures the SORTEE guidelines group under
Stage 5: wrong paths, missing packages and missing files ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}). It
will not catch Stage 6 failures, such as stochasticity and version sensitivity.
Those need a seed and a documented environment.
:::

## A project layout that works {#quickstart-layout}

The two conventions in the tree below come from
[Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023, §3.1)]{.tada-cite data-key="ivimey-cook-2023"}.

::: {.tada-wiki}
The layout itself is our own suggestion. The exact layout matters less than whether
a reader can see the order and purpose of every file without asking you.
:::

```
my-project/
├── README.md                 <- start here: what this is, how to run it
├── LICENSE                   <- how others may use the code
├── my-project.Rproj          <- or a Python virtual environment
├── data/
│   ├── raw/                  <- never edited by any script
│   │   └── caterpillars_2024.csv
│   └── processed/            <- written by 01_, read by 02_
│       └── caterpillars_clean.csv
├── R/                        <- or scripts/, or src/
│   ├── 01_clean_data.R
│   ├── 02_fit_models.R
│   └── 03_make_figures.R
├── functions/                <- helpers sourced by the scripts above
│   └── utils.R
└── output/
    ├── figures/
    └── models/               <- saved model objects for slow fits
```

Two conventions do most of the work.

1. **Numbered scripts.** A reader knows the order to run things in without
   being told: `01_`, `02_`, `03_`.
2. **`data/raw/` is read-only.** Cleaning writes to `data/processed/`. Raw data
   are never modified or overwritten by a script, so a botched cleaning step
   cannot destroy the original.

## Three common causes of failure {#quickstart-mistakes}

The first two rows come from the TADA guidelines and the third from the
SORTEE guidelines ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}, Stage 6).

| Mistake | Why it breaks | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `setwd("C:/Users/ed/Desktop/analysis")` | The path exists on exactly one computer | Open the project through its `.Rproj` file, or start Python inside the project folder, and build paths with `here()` / `pyprojroot` |
| Code shared as a `.pdf` or `.docx` | Copy-pasting silently mangles apostrophes, quotes and whitespace, and drags in line numbers and headers | Save as `.R` / `.py` |
| No `set.seed()` before a simulation or MCMC run | Results change every run, so nobody can tell a real mismatch from noise | Set a seed at the top of each independently runnable section |

::: {.tada-warn}
People underestimate the `.pdf` and `.docx` problem. Copying code out of these
formats can change characters (curly apostrophes for straight ones) and white
space (non-breaking spaces for ordinary ones). The code still *looks* right, so
the errors can be hard to spot and slow to fix.
:::

## The README {#quickstart-readme}

Copy [`templates/README-template.md`](templates/README-template.md) into your
project and replace the angle-bracketed parts. The
[Documented](#documented-readme) chapter explains each field and why it is
there.

Or generate one with [READMEBuilder](https://github.com/EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder) (`devtools::install_github("EIvimeyCook/READMEBuilder")`, then `build_readme()`), a Shiny app that fills in these fields from your project and writes the `README.md`.

## What happens next {#quickstart-next}

::: {.tada-dog-float .tada-dog-float--standalone .is-happy}
![](assets/figures/dog-happy.png){.tada-dog-happy alt="A happy cartoon dog wearing a wizard hat"}
:::


If your target journal has a **data editor**, someone will check your deposit
against something close to the [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) ([Pick et al. 2026]{.tada-cite data-key="pick-2026"}).
These have six stages, from whether the code is archived under a licence to
whether the results reproduce. Read that section to see what the checks
are before they are applied to your submission.

If your journal has no data editor, the checks still matter. They fall to you
and your co-authors, through [code review](#code-review).
